newsitem.title: UK: Aluminium stocks expected to rise.
newsitem.headline: Aluminium stocks expected to rise.

text.p: London Metal Exchange (LME) aluminium stocks are expected to rise sharply over the coming weeks as the expanding backwardation attracts metal to warehouses, traders say.

One LME trader, who said that 50,000 tonnes of off-warrant material is scheduled to arrive in LME warehouses in the short term, said he expected around 3,000 tonnes per day to be put back on warrant this week.
Analysts said they would not be surprised to see a hefty increase in aluminium stocks, but added that this would not cause a reassessment of the demand-supply balance.
A rise in stocks was to be expected as a realignment after an unexpectedly high stock drawdown in the first half of this year, according to Raju Daswani of Metal Bulletin Research (MBR).
Daswani said that the decline in inventories had been some 100,000 tonnes too much, and that a correction in the third quarter would be followed by a further reduction in the fourth quarter.
Stocks fell by 425 tonnes on Tuesday after a 6,650-tonne rise on Monday which some analysts attributed to seasonal demand weakness.
Stocks bounced up on August 12 after reaching a low of 620,147 tonnes the previous day, at the end of a sustained decline which began in January and reduced inventories by 36 percent.
Despite this, the fundamentals are still firm for aluminium, and overall supplies are still being depleted, analysts said.
"The movement in total industry stocks is definitely down. The market is clearly in deficit." said Alan Williamson of Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.
"You have to go back to June 1987 to find a stock-consumption ration so low with stocks still falling," Williamson said, adding that this had been the precursor to a sharp run up in prices in 1988.
The movement of stocks is seen to be crucial to a market which was weakened by a general sell-off in base metals on Monday after a sharp drop in the Dow.

"If a backwardation can be achieved for a further two to three weeks, and the rate of metal deliveries fails to slow, then it is bearish. However, if over this period the metal arrivals slow and perhaps draws are seen, then this would be a very bullish sign indeed," said GNI Research.
MBR is forecasting a deficit of 230,000 tonnes in 1997 and spot prices averaging $1,620.
"Demand outlook remains very firm. We continue to forecast inventory erosion throughout the balance of the year," said Flemings Research. -- London Newsroom +44 171 542 8071
